summary.text: The Middle Ages, or medieval period, is the stretch of European history lasting from about the 5th to the late 15th centuries.
It is the middle of three traditional divisions of Western history, between classical antiquity and the modern period, and is split into Early, High, and Late Middle Ages.
It began with the fall of the Western Roman Empire and passed into the modern age during the Renaissance, the Reformation, and the Age of Discovery.

items.prompt: A friend asks why the era is called the "Middle" Ages and not something else. Which explanation fits best?

options.label: Europe sat at the centre of world trade at that time
It sits between classical antiquity and the modern period
The people living then called their own time the middle age
It lay halfway between Rome's founding and the present day

items.explain: History is traditionally divided into classical antiquity, the medieval period, and the modern period, so the medieval sits in the middle. Medieval people themselves called their times modern.

items.prompt: A monk in the 1200s is asked what sort of age he lives in. Going by how medieval writers saw their time, what would he most likely say?

options.label: A long gap between Rome and a coming revival
A dark age that followed the light of Rome
A modern age, and the last one before the world's end
A new Roman age under a restored empire

items.explain: Medieval writers called their own times modern and thought theirs was the last period before the end of the world. The ideas of a "middle" age and a "dark" age came from later writers.

items.prompt: A historian explains why Europe had fewer people at the end of the medieval period than earlier. What does she point to?

options.label: Famine, plague, and war hitting the Late Middle Ages
Viking, Magyar, and Saracen raids on the Carolingian realm
Warm weather that cut harvests and emptied the towns
The Crusades, which drained every kingdom of its people

items.explain: The Late Middle Ages brought famine, plague, and war, which significantly cut Europe's population. Warm weather actually helped crop yields earlier, and the raids hit the Carolingian Empire.

items.prompt: In the High Middle Ages, a village harvests more from the same land than its grandparents did, and its market keeps growing. What helped?

options.label: Weaker kings who left villages to run themselves
The split of the Christian church in 1054
Mass migrations of tribes into the old empire
Technological and agricultural advances, plus a warmer climate

items.explain: Technological and agricultural innovations let trade flourish, and the Medieval Warm Period raised crop yields, so Europe's population grew significantly.

items.prompt: A peasant owes rent and labour to a local noble, while a knight owes military service to his overlord. Which pair of terms names these two arrangements?

options.label: Feudalism for the peasant, manorialism for the knight
Scholasticism for the peasant, feudalism for the knight
Manorialism for the peasant, feudalism for the knight
Manorialism for both the peasant and the knight

items.explain: Manorialism organised peasants into villages owing rent and labour to nobles. Feudalism was the political structure in which knights owed military service in return for the right to rent from lands.

items.prompt: One historian says the Middle Ages ended in 1453 and another says 1492. Why can both be defended?

options.label: No end date is agreed on, and different events get used
One is simply wrong, because it ended exactly in 1500
The first date fits Europe and the second only fits Asia
The period ended in the West earlier than in the East

items.explain: For Europe as a whole 1500 is often used, but no end date is universally agreed. Depending on context, events such as the conquest of Constantinople in 1453 or Columbus's first voyage in 1492 are used.

beats.title: Europe's long middle chapter
beats.hook: Nobody agrees on exactly when it ended, yet it shaped the way we split up all of history.

beats.prompt: Put these medieval events in the order they happened.

items.label: The Carolingian Empire is briefly established
The East-West Schism splits the Christian church

beats.explain: The Carolingian Empire came in the later 8th and early 9th centuries, the Schism in 1054, the first Crusade preaching in 1095, and the Black Death in 1347 to 1350.

beats.prompt: Match each medieval idea to what it describes.

right.label: Knights owing military service to their overlords
A philosophy joining faith to reason
Peasants in villages owing rent and labour to nobles
Attempts to regain the Holy Land from Muslims

beats.explain: Each is a feature of medieval life: how land and work were organised, how rulers were served, how scholars thought, and how Western Christians fought.

beats.prompt: In the High Middle Ages, farming and technology improve, trade flourishes, and the climate turns warmer. What happens to Europe's population?
beats.explain: Technological and agricultural innovations let trade flourish and the warmer climate raised yields, so the population grew significantly.

choices.label: It stays the same, because farmland is limited
choices.feedback: Limits sound plausible, but innovations and warmer weather raised crop yields.

choices.label: It falls, because trade crowds people together
choices.feedback: Crowding sounds risky, but the sources link trade and better crop yields to growth, not decline.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about when the Middle Ages ended is wrong. Which?

steps.text: The Middle Ages began with the fall of the Western Roman Empire.
Every historian uses the same single year for the end.
English historians often mark the end with the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485.
So the end date depends on the context.

beats.explain: There is no universally agreed end date. Dates like 1485 for English historians or 1492 for Spain are used depending on context.

beats.idea: The Middle Ages is the middle of a three-part scheme of European history, running from Rome's fall to the modern age, with farming, faith, and plague shaping it.

paragraphs.heading: The middle of three ages
paragraphs.text: In European history, the Middle Ages, also called the medieval period, ran roughly from the 5th century to the late 15th. Western history is traditionally cut into three parts: classical antiquity, then this medieval stretch, then the modern period. The Middle Ages are split again into an Early, a High and a Late phase. They opened with the fall of the Western Roman Empire and faded into the modern age through the Reformation, the Renaissance, the Age of Discovery and Europe's wars of religion.

paragraphs.heading: The Early Middle Ages
paragraphs.text: Falling populations, the breakdown of central government, invasions and mass migrations began in late antiquity and carried on into the Early Middle Ages. Germanic peoples on the move founded new kingdoms in what was left of the Western Roman Empire. In the east, the Byzantine Empire, the direct heir of Rome, lived on as a major power. In the later 8th and early 9th centuries the Franks briefly built the Carolingian Empire across much of Western Europe. It later gave way under civil wars and attacks by Vikings, Magyars and Saracens.

paragraphs.heading: The High Middle Ages
paragraphs.text: After the year 1000, Europe's population grew a great deal. New techniques in farming and technology let trade thrive, and a warmer climate, the Medieval Warm Period, raised harvests. Two systems shaped society. Under manorialism, peasants lived in villages and owed rent and work to nobles; under feudalism, knights and lesser nobles owed military service to their lords in return for income from land. Thinkers practised scholasticism, which tried to join faith with reason, and universities were founded.

paragraphs.heading: Schism and Crusade
paragraphs.text: The single Christian church broke apart in the East–West Schism of 1054. The Crusades, first preached in 1095, were armed efforts by Western European Christians to take the Holy Land back from Muslims. Kings meanwhile came to rule centralised nation-states, which cut crime and violence but made a single united Christendom harder to imagine.

paragraphs.heading: The Late Middle Ages
paragraphs.text: The last phase brought hunger, disease and war, which sharply reduced Europe's population. Between 1347 and 1350 the Black Death alone killed about one European in three. Quarrels and splits inside the Catholic Church ran alongside wars between states, civil strife and peasant uprisings. Cultural and technical change then reshaped European society and opened the early modern period.

paragraphs.heading: No agreed finish line
paragraphs.text: Around 500 is the usual starting point, and Bruni first used 476, when the last Roman emperor in the West was removed and replaced by a German chieftain. The end is less settled. For Europe as a whole 1500 is common, but some prefer the Turkish capture of Constantinople in 1453, Columbus's first voyage in 1492 or the Reformation in 1517. English historians often choose the Battle of Bosworth Field in 1485.
